title: Requests and Commitments in Email are More Complex Than You Think: Eight Reasons to be Cautious
research_question: Which recurring phenomena make requests and commitments in real workplace email difficult to annotate or extract reliably, and what annotation principles are needed to handle those phenomena consistently?
methodology: The paper synthesizes observations from a series of three-annotator experiments on randomly sampled messages from the processed Enron corpus, including sentence-level experiments with 54 messages and 310 sentences and later 350 messages and 750 sentences, plus a 100-message message-level experiment. The authors compare interannotator agreement across these experiments and perform qualitative analysis of recurrent ambiguous cases. They organize the resulting problems into eight edge-case categories and specify operational annotation principles designed for a high-recall email application that highlights potentially useful requests and commitments.

key_findings.finding: More explicit guidance for conditional and indirect phenomena coincided with a large improvement in commitment agreement: three-way commitment kappa increased from 0.54 in the first sentence experiment to 0.74 in the second, while request kappa changed from 0.78 to 0.80.
Message-level annotation yielded still higher agreement, with kappa 0.84 for requests and 0.78 for commitments; the paper links part of this gain to avoiding sentence-level locus ambiguity.
key_findings.section: 3 The Data and Annotation Experiments and 4.1 Locus Ambiguity

key_findings.finding: The authors identify eight systematic edge-case categories: locus ambiguity, meetings, pleasantries, requests for inaction, process instructions, attachment-review requests, reported requests and commitments, and third-party commitments that also function as requests.
key_findings.section: 4 Edge Case Phenomena in Email and 5 Conclusions

key_findings.finding: Several categories cannot be classified reliably from surface wording alone and instead require message context, intended recipient information, or knowledge about whether an obligation is actually imposed.
key_findings.section: 4 Edge Case Phenomena in Email and 5 Conclusions

key_findings.finding: The same underlying obligation may have multiple direct or indirect sentence realizations, so the authors' high-recall scheme marks every sentence that realizes a request or commitment rather than forcing a single textual locus.
A commitment can simultaneously be a request when it places an obligation on an email recipient; the paper therefore rejects mutually exclusive speech-act labeling for such cases.

The intended downstream application affects what should count as relevant: highlighting obligations in-place, extracting a task list, and producing an action-oriented thread summary can legitimately require different annotation decisions.

The authors argue that evaluation against a single objective gold standard is problematic when human interpretation itself is ambiguous, and propose real-user mailbox and task contexts as more meaningful but less repeatable evaluation settings.

limitations: The empirical observations come primarily from the Enron corpus, so organizational culture, period, and email style may limit generalization.
The eight-category taxonomy is grounded in the authors' annotation experience but is not demonstrated to be exhaustive.
Several recommended labels intentionally depend on the chosen high-recall application and therefore are conventions rather than universally valid speech-act definitions.
Some categories, including process instructions and reported requests or commitments, remain explicitly dependent on annotator judgment.
The processed Enron dump used for experiments contains message bodies without attachments even though attachment-related requests are discussed as an important workplace-email phenomenon.
The paper reports annotation agreement rather than performance of an implemented automatic extraction system.
Reliable classification may require private user, relationship, task, or organizational context that is unavailable in standard corpora.
The authors acknowledge that user-context evaluation raises privacy, data-access, and repeatability problems.
raw_claims: The paper bases its analysis on several manual annotation experiments over randomly sampled Enron email.
The first sentence experiment reported request kappa 0.78 and commitment kappa 0.54.
A later sentence experiment reported request kappa 0.80 and commitment kappa 0.74 after more explicit annotation guidance.
Message-level annotation reported request kappa 0.84 and commitment kappa 0.78.
Locus ambiguity occurs when the same request or commitment is realized in more than one sentence or has no obvious single sentence locus.
The annotation scheme treats meeting announcements as implicit requests to attend.
Pleasantries are excluded when they do not create a meaningful obligation.
Requests for inaction are still treated as requests because they impose an obligation not to act.
Process instructions and reported obligations may require local context and annotator judgment.
An attachment counts as a request only when accompanying message text can be interpreted as requesting something about it.
A third-party commitment can also be labeled a request when the committed party is a recipient and therefore receives an obligation.
The authors conclude that many request and commitment phenomena require contextual rather than purely surface-form modeling.
The paper states that an email collection independently labeled by five annotators according to its guidelines was available for download.
